title: Senior Platform Engineer (AWS Focus)
tagline: Build the paved road so every AI team at the bank can ship agents on AWS without reinventing security, networking, or FinOps.
overview: This is not an 'AI engineer' role — it's a platform engineer whose customers happen to be AI teams. A large fintech like XYZ Bank needs someone who can turn Bedrock, SageMaker, EKS and the rest of the AWS AI stack into governed, repeatable, self-service building blocks that dozens of application teams can consume without each of them re-deriving IAM boundaries, network isolation, or cost controls from scratch. The job is equal parts landing-zone architecture, Terraform module engineering, and FinOps discipline, with AI orchestration as the workload it exists to serve. Interviewers are probing for three things: can you actually design multi-account AWS environments and reusable IaC at enterprise scale (not just write a Lambda function), do you understand the specific security and residency constraints of running GenAI in a regulated bank, and can you talk fluently about tradeoffs (EKS vs Lambda, API Gateway vs Kong, Bedrock vs SageMaker) rather than reciting service names. A strong candidate frames every answer around 'platform as a product' — versioned contracts, self-service onboarding, and guardrails baked into the pipeline — and is explicit about where they've had to balance developer velocity against a bank's security and audit requirements.

sections.heading: Landing Zones & Multi-Account Platform Strategy
sections.summary: Covers how to structure a multi-account AWS estate from scratch and how to package platform capabilities as products rather than one-off builds — the foundational architecture question for this role.

content.text: A landing zone is the governed multi-account baseline everything else sits on: identity, guardrails (preventive via SCPs, detective via AWS Config), centralized logging, and network foundations, usually stood up with AWS Control Tower and extended with Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) so account vending is code-driven instead of click-driven. For an AI platform team, the landing zone question isn't just 'how do we organize accounts' — it's 'how do we isolate blast radius and compliance scope for AI workloads specifically,' since Bedrock/SageMaker traffic, model data, and PII often carry stricter regulatory scope than a typical microservice.

rows: No workloads deployed here; break-glass access only
S3 Object Lock, cross-account write-only from spokes
Transit Gateway, Direct Connect, Route 53 Resolver, shared VPC endpoints
Central egress, PrivateLink hub for Bedrock/SageMaker endpoints
Bedrock/SageMaker platform accounts, model registries, shared Knowledge Base infra
Cross-account sharing via AWS RAM and resource policies, not credential sharing
SCPs enforce tagging, region lock, encryption; per-account budgets
No path to prod data; auto-expiring accounts

items: Tenancy pattern A — hub-and-spoke: a central AI platform account hosts shared Bedrock Knowledge Bases, Guardrails, and model access; workload accounts consume them cross-account via resource policies and AWS RAM shares. Good for consistent governance and shared cost pools.

Tenancy pattern B — per-tenant/account-per-product: each AI product gets its own account from the same Terraform module set, giving hard IAM/network isolation at the cost of more duplicated infrastructure. Common where regulatory segregation (e.g. distinct legal entities or PCI scope) demands it.
Most enterprise platforms end up hybrid: shared hub for expensive, hard-to-replicate primitives (Guardrails, vector stores, model access), account-per-tenant for compute and data planes.

Productizing the platform means treating each capability (landing zone vend, EKS cluster, Bedrock agent scaffold) as a versioned product: a name, a contract (inputs/outputs, SLAs), an owner, a changelog, and a self-service entry point (Service Catalog, internal portal, or `terraform apply` against a published module) — not a wiki page and a Slack channel.

content.text: In interviews, be ready to defend why you picked a given account structure for a specific compliance boundary (e.g. keeping cardholder-data-adjacent workloads in a separate OU with tighter SCPs) rather than describing Control Tower generically.

interviewQA.q: Walk me through how you'd design the account structure for a new AI platform inside an existing AWS Organization.
interviewQA.a: I'd start from the bank's existing Control Tower landing zone rather than reinvent it — add an AI Platform OU under the standard structure with a hub account for shared, expensive-to-duplicate primitives like Bedrock Knowledge Bases and Guardrails, and let application teams get their own workload accounts vended through Account Factory for Terraform so it's code, not a ticket. I'd separate dev/test/prod at the account level, not just by tag, because SCPs and IAM boundaries are the real blast-radius control. Anything touching card or customer PII gets its own OU with tighter SCPs — region lock, mandatory encryption, no public egress. The goal is that a new AI product team can request an account and get a compliant baseline in hours, not weeks.

interviewQA.q: Why use a hub-and-spoke tenancy pattern instead of just replicating full infrastructure per team?
interviewQA.a: Some things are genuinely expensive or risky to duplicate — Bedrock Guardrails configuration, shared vector stores, model access approvals — so centralizing those in a hub account and sharing them cross-account via resource policies and AWS RAM keeps governance consistent and audit-friendly. But I don't push everything into the hub; compute and data planes stay in the tenant's own account so a bug or breach in one product doesn't cross-contaminate another. It's a judgment call per capability, not a blanket pattern.

interviewQA.q: How do you 'productize' a platform service instead of just building infrastructure for one team and calling it done?
interviewQA.a: I treat it like a product: give it a name, a versioned interface — inputs, outputs, SLAs — and an owner who takes support tickets. Concretely that means a Terraform module in a private registry with semantic versioning, a Service Catalog or internal portal entry so teams self-serve without opening a ticket, and a changelog so consumers know what changed between versions. I also instrument usage so I know who's actually using it, which drives the deprecation and investment roadmap.

interviewQA.q: A business unit says their workload can't share the central AI platform account for regulatory reasons. How do you handle that?
interviewQA.a: I take that seriously rather than fight it — regulatory segregation is a legitimate reason to break the hub-and-spoke pattern. I'd stand up a dedicated account from the same Terraform module catalog so they get an isolated Bedrock/SageMaker footprint with their own KMS keys and network path, but still consume the same versioned modules and CI/CD patterns as everyone else. That keeps operational consistency even when tenancy isolation requirements differ.

interviewQA.q: What's the difference between preventive and detective controls in a landing zone, and where do Bedrock-specific risks fit?
interviewQA.a: Preventive controls are SCPs and permission boundaries that make a bad action impossible — for example, blocking Bedrock model invocation in regions outside our approved list, or denying public S3 buckets outright. Detective controls, like AWS Config rules and Security Hub findings, catch things after the fact — a Knowledge Base data source pointing at an unencrypted bucket, for instance. For GenAI specifically I lean preventive wherever I can, because the cost of a data leak through a misconfigured Knowledge Base or an over-permissioned agent is high, and detective controls are the safety net, not the primary defense.

sections.heading: AI Service Orchestration: Bedrock, SageMaker & Applied AI Services
sections.summary: Covers when to reach for Bedrock vs SageMaker vs the applied AI services (Rekognition, Textract), and the current state of Bedrock's agentic building blocks — Agents, Knowledge Bases, Guardrails.

content.text: Bedrock is the API layer: managed access to foundation models plus the scaffolding to build agents (Agents for Bedrock — a planner, an action-group registry backed by Lambda, optional memory, and Knowledge Base attachment), managed RAG (Knowledge Bases, which now includes a fully-managed option covering embeddings, vector storage and re-ranking without you standing up OpenSearch yourself), and policy enforcement (Guardrails — content filters, denied topics, PII/sensitive-info redaction, and as of 2026 an `InvokeGuardrailChecks` API for step-level checks inside agentic loops, including inspecting code, tool arguments and function names for injected instructions). SageMaker is the full ML platform: training, fine-tuning, custom model hosting, pipelines, feature store, and now SageMaker Unified Studio, which has narrowed the UX gap with Bedrock but still targets teams that need to bring their own data and control the training loop.

rows: You need a foundation model fast, with managed RAG and policy controls, no training data of your own
Customer-facing chat assistant grounded on product T&Cs via Knowledge Bases
You have labeled/proprietary data, need custom or fine-tuned models, or strict data-residency control over the training loop
Fraud/credit-risk scoring model trained on the bank's own transaction history
Image/video analysis — identity verification, document image quality, content moderation
Selfie-vs-ID liveness check during digital onboarding
Structured extraction from scanned/PDF documents — forms, tables, key-value pairs
KYC document and invoice ingestion pipeline
Formerly used for automated anomaly detection on business metrics — AWS ended support Oct 10, 2025
Migrate existing use cases to CloudWatch anomaly detection, OpenSearch, Redshift ML, or Glue Data Quality

items: Default rule of thumb: start with Bedrock for time-to-market; move a workload to SageMaker only when you have a concrete reason — labeled training data, a domain-specific fine-tune, or a data-sovereignty constraint that a managed multi-tenant inference service can't satisfy.

Multi-agent collaboration in Bedrock (supervisor agent delegating to collaborator agents) is the pattern to know for anything beyond single-turn Q&A — it maps well onto 'triage agent hands off to a specialist agent' workflows common in claims or loan processing.

Guardrails should be treated as a platform-owned, centrally versioned artifact (like an IAM policy), not something each app team configures ad hoc — that's how you keep denied-topic and PII policies consistent across every AI product in the bank.

Be ready to note that Lookout for Metrics is deprecated — naming it in the JD without flagging the end-of-support date is a common trap; a strong candidate corrects the record and proposes the AWS-recommended replacement path.

content.text: The interview signal here is less 'do you know the API surface' and more 'do you have a decision framework' — expect to be asked to justify a Bedrock-vs-SageMaker call for a specific fintech scenario, not just list features.

interviewQA.q: When would you tell an application team to use SageMaker instead of Bedrock?
interviewQA.a: When they have proprietary labeled data and a real reason to train or fine-tune rather than prompt — a credit-risk or fraud model trained on the bank's own transaction history is the classic case, because a foundation model's general knowledge isn't the differentiator there, the bank's data is. I'd also push toward SageMaker if there's a hard data-residency requirement that a shared multi-tenant inference endpoint can't satisfy, or if the workload is tabular/structured rather than language-based. Otherwise I default teams to Bedrock because it gets them to production faster with far less infrastructure to own.

interviewQA.q: The JD lists 'Lookout' as a service to operationalize. What would you flag about that?
interviewQA.a: I'd point out that AWS ended support for Amazon Lookout for Metrics on October 10, 2025, so if that's the service they mean, we shouldn't be building new dependencies on it — AWS's guidance is to move anomaly-detection use cases to CloudWatch anomaly detection, OpenSearch, Redshift ML, QuickSight, or Glue Data Quality depending on the data shape. I'd want to clarify with the team whether they meant Lookout for Metrics specifically or were using it as shorthand for 'anomaly detection,' and then propose the right modern replacement rather than standing up a deprecated service.

interviewQA.q: How do Bedrock Guardrails fit into a multi-team platform, and who should own them?
interviewQA.a: I treat Guardrails as a platform-owned, versioned artifact rather than something each application team configures for themselves — the same way we centrally own IAM permission boundaries. That gives us one place to enforce denied-topic policies, PII redaction, and content filtering consistently, and it means a compliance change (say, a new denied topic mandated by legal) rolls out to every consumer through a module version bump instead of chasing a dozen teams. For agentic workloads specifically, I'd also use the step-level guardrail checks introduced in 2026 so tool calls and code the agent generates get inspected, not just the final response.

interviewQA.q: Explain the difference between Bedrock Knowledge Bases and standing up your own RAG pipeline.
interviewQA.a: Knowledge Bases is Bedrock's managed RAG offering — it handles ingestion, chunking, embedding, vector storage, and retrieval, and as of the 2026 managed option it can run the vector store and re-ranking for you too, so you're not operating OpenSearch Serverless or Aurora pgvector yourself. I'd reach for it by default for standard document-grounded assistants. I'd only build a custom RAG pipeline if I needed retrieval logic Knowledge Bases doesn't support yet — a very specific hybrid search strategy, or a vector store we already run for other reasons — because owning that pipeline is real operational overhead I don't want to hand every app team.

interviewQA.q: Describe a multi-agent pattern you'd use for something like loan or claims processing.
interviewQA.a: I'd use Bedrock's multi-agent collaboration pattern — a supervisor agent that takes the initial request and delegates to specialist collaborator agents: one for document extraction via Textract, one for policy/eligibility checks grounded on a Knowledge Base of underwriting rules, and one for fraud-risk scoring that might call out to a SageMaker endpoint. The supervisor owns the conversation and final decision, and Guardrails wrap every step so a jailbreak attempt against one specialist agent doesn't propagate. This mirrors how a real underwriting team is organized, which makes it easier to explain to business stakeholders too.

interviewQA.q: Where does Rekognition or Textract actually add value over a general foundation model doing the same task?
interviewQA.a: They're purpose-built and cheaper for narrow, high-volume tasks — Textract's form and table extraction is more reliable and far less costly than asking a multimodal foundation model to OCR a document at scale, and Rekognition's face-comparison APIs for selfie-vs-ID liveness checks are tuned specifically for that identity-verification use case with predictable latency, in the seconds range, that a general model wouldn't guarantee. I'd use a foundation model when the task genuinely needs reasoning over the extracted content, and Rekognition/Textract as the deterministic front-end that feeds it clean structured data.

sections.heading: Infrastructure as Code: Versioned Terraform Modules & Platform APIs
sections.summary: Covers how to structure, version, validate and release Terraform modules as products — the mechanism that actually delivers 'platform as a product' at scale.

content.text: Standardizing on Terraform isn't the interesting part of this responsibility — module design, versioning discipline, and release management are. A platform team's Terraform modules are a public API to every other engineering team in the bank, so they need the same rigor as any published SDK: semantic versioning, a changelog, backwards-compatibility guarantees within a major version, and automated validation before anything reaches a private registry.

content.code:
# Example: consuming a versioned platform module for a Bedrock agent
module "bedrock_agent" {
  source  = "app.terraform.io/adcb-platform/bedrock-agent/aws"
  version = "~> 2.4.0"  # pessimistic constraint: patch/minor auto-upgrades, major requires a deliberate bump

  agent_name         = "claims-triage-agent"
  foundation_model    = "anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5-v1:0"
  guardrail_id        = module.guardrails.guardrail_id
  knowledge_base_ids  = [module.kb_claims.knowledge_base_id]
  action_group_lambda = module.claims_lookup_fn.function_arn

  vpc_config = {
    subnet_ids         = module.network.private_subnet_ids
    security_group_ids = [module.network.agent_sg_id]
  }

  tags = local.mandatory_tags  # enforced by Sentinel/OPA policy check in CI
}

rows: VPC, IAM boundary, KMS key, landing-zone account vend
Platform team only, rarely touched directly
New teams copy as a starting point, then pin to real modules
Internal CLI, Service Catalog product, Backstage template
Non-Terraform-fluent teams who just want 'give me an agent runtime'

items: Validation pipeline: pre-commit `terraform fmt`/`validate` → `tflint` → `checkov`/`tfsec` for security misconfig → policy-as-code (OPA/Conftest or Sentinel) enforcing tagging, encryption, and no-public-ingress rules → `terraform plan` posted to the PR → Terratest or `terraform test` for module-level behavioral assertions.
Commit the `.terraform.lock.hcl` file so provider versions are reproducible across every consumer; fail CI if a provider version is unpinned.

Release management: tag modules with semver, publish to a private registry (Terraform Cloud/Enterprise or a Git-tag-based source), maintain a changelog, and use Renovate/Dependabot to open automated upgrade PRs against consumers rather than expecting every team to poll for new versions.

For teams that don't want to write HCL at all, wrap the modules behind a Service Catalog product or an internal Backstage-style software template — that's the 'platform API' half of the responsibility, not just the Terraform itself.

interviewQA.q: How do you structure Terraform modules so dozens of teams can consume them safely?
interviewQA.a: I layer them: foundational modules for things like VPC and KMS that the platform team owns exclusively, composite product modules like a Bedrock agent scaffold or an EKS agent runtime that app teams consume directly via a pinned version, and reference implementations that show a fully wired example a new team can copy from. Every consumer-facing module gets semantic versioning with a pessimistic constraint like `~> 2.4.0` so they get patch and minor fixes automatically but a major version bump — which might change variable names or defaults — requires a deliberate decision. That's what lets me evolve the platform without breaking twenty teams at once.

interviewQA.q: What does your Terraform validation pipeline actually check before a module release?
interviewQA.a: Format and syntax first with `terraform fmt` and `validate`, then `tflint` for provider-specific correctness, then `checkov` or `tfsec` for security misconfigurations like public S3 buckets or overly broad security groups. On top of that I run policy-as-code — OPA or Sentinel — to enforce organizational rules that are non-negotiable in a bank: mandatory tags for cost allocation, encryption-at-rest everywhere, no public ingress on anything touching customer data. Finally I run Terratest or native `terraform test` to assert the module actually produces the resources and outputs it claims to, not just that it's syntactically valid.

interviewQA.q: A downstream team says a module version bump broke their deployment. How do you prevent that going forward?
interviewQA.a: First I'd fix their immediate break, but the real fix is process: I enforce semantic versioning strictly, so a breaking change is only ever a major version bump, never hidden in a patch or minor release. I maintain a changelog and, for major versions, a migration guide. And I use automated dependency-update tooling like Renovate so consumers get small, frequent, low-risk version bumps instead of falling years behind and then hitting a wall of accumulated breaking changes all at once.

interviewQA.q: Why version and publish Terraform modules through a private registry instead of just having teams reference a Git path?
interviewQA.a: A Git path with no tag pinning means every `terraform init` can silently pull a different commit, which is exactly the reproducibility problem versioning is supposed to solve. A private registry with semver gives me the same guarantees a language package registry gives — explicit version constraints, a discoverable module catalog, and a clear place to publish release notes. It also lets me gate publishing behind the validation pipeline, so nothing reaches a version tag that hasn't passed security and policy checks.

interviewQA.q: How do you help a team that isn't comfortable writing Terraform directly consume the platform?
interviewQA.a: That's what I mean by a platform API, not just modules — I'll wrap the common patterns behind a Service Catalog product or an internal developer portal template where they fill in a short form (agent name, model, data sources) and the pipeline runs the underlying Terraform for them, pinned to a known-good module version. They get self-service without needing HCL fluency, and I still get the guardrails and versioning benefits underneath, because it's the same modules doing the actual provisioning.

sections.heading: Runtime Patterns: EKS, Lambda & Event-Driven Agent Workloads
sections.summary: Covers the compute and event-processing tradeoffs for AI/agent workloads — when Lambda is the right shape, when it isn't, and how EventBridge/SQS/Step Functions hold resilient pipelines together.

content.text: The honest framing for this section is: match the architecture to the workload, not to a preference. Lambda is the default for lightweight, short-lived work — the tool/action-group functions a Bedrock agent calls, event handlers, glue code — with a warm invocation calling a fast model landing around 300ms end-to-end. But multi-step agentic workflows regularly exceed Lambda's 15-minute timeout, need GPU-backed custom inference, or run at sustained high throughput where reserved container capacity is materially cheaper than pay-per-invocation — that's EKS (or ECS/Fargate) territory. EventBridge, SQS and Step Functions are the connective tissue that make either compute layer resilient under failure.

rows: Low for warm invocations (~300ms typical for a light Bedrock call)
No cold start once pods are running, but pod scheduling adds its own latency
Pay-per-invocation; can exceed container cost at sustained high throughput
Reserved/Spot capacity cheaper at steady, high-volume load
Action-group tool calls, event handlers, light orchestration glue
Long-running multi-agent sessions, GPU inference, service-mesh-integrated workloads, Karpenter-driven autoscaling
Real — cluster upgrades, node groups, mesh, RBAC

items: Step Functions as the 'outer loop' for long-running AI workflows: Wait states for human-in-the-loop approval (e.g. a loan decision above a threshold), Map state for parallel document extraction across a batch, and native retry/catch for transient Bedrock throttling.

SQS between event producer and consumer decouples burst traffic from downstream capacity, and a dead-letter queue on every agent-invocation queue is non-negotiable — a stuck or malformed agent request should never silently disappear.

EventBridge with a dedicated custom event bus (not the default bus) for AI-platform events makes cross-account event routing and access control explicit via event bus resource policies, and keeps the noisy default AWS-service event stream separate.
For real-time fraud/risk scoring alongside agent workloads, Kinesis Data Streams (or MSK) suits continuous, ordered, replayable event ingestion better than SQS.

interviewQA.q: When would you push back on a team that wants to run their agent orchestration entirely on Lambda?
interviewQA.a: If their agent workflow is multi-step and could realistically run past 15 minutes — waiting on a human approval, chaining several tool calls with retries — Lambda's timeout will eventually bite them in production, usually under load rather than in testing. I'd walk them through moving the long-running orchestration into Step Functions, which has no such ceiling and gives native retry/catch semantics, while keeping the individual tool-call functions as Lambda since those genuinely are short-lived. It's not about banning Lambda, it's about not using it for the piece of the architecture it's the wrong shape for.

interviewQA.q: Explain how you'd design a resilient event-driven pipeline for asynchronous agent invocations.
interviewQA.a: I'd put a dedicated EventBridge custom bus in front so I can control access via bus policies rather than mixing AI-platform events into the default bus. Events fan out to Step Functions for anything multi-step, or directly to Lambda for simple handlers, and every queue in the path has a dead-letter queue so a malformed or repeatedly-failing message gets surfaced instead of silently dropped or endlessly retried. I'd also add CloudWatch alarms on DLQ depth so an operational issue pages someone before customers notice, not after.

interviewQA.q: What's the cost tradeoff between Lambda and EKS for a sustained, high-throughput agent workload?
interviewQA.a: Lambda's pay-per-invocation model is great for spiky or low-volume traffic because you pay nothing when idle, but at sustained high throughput the per-invocation cost can add up to more than reserved or Spot container capacity on EKS running the same workload continuously. So for something like a fraud-scoring agent handling constant transaction volume, I'd model both costs at expected steady-state load before deciding, rather than defaulting to serverless because it's operationally simpler — simplicity and cost-efficiency aren't the same axis.

interviewQA.q: How do Step Functions help specifically with human-in-the-loop requirements common in banking workflows?
interviewQA.a: Step Functions has a native Wait-for-callback pattern — a task can pause and wait for an external system, like a case-management UI where a loan officer approves an above-threshold decision, to call back with a task token before the state machine continues. That gives me a durable, resumable pause without polling or keeping a Lambda alive burning cost while waiting on a human. It also gives me a visual execution history, which is genuinely useful evidence for an audit trail in a regulated environment.

interviewQA.q: Why put a custom EventBridge bus in front of the AI platform instead of using the account's default bus?
interviewQA.a: The default bus is shared with every AWS-service-generated event in the account, which makes access control and noise filtering harder. A dedicated bus lets me write a resource policy scoped specifically to which accounts and roles can publish or subscribe to AI-platform events, which matters when I'm sharing agent-completion events across multiple workload accounts in a hub-and-spoke tenancy model. It's a small design choice but it makes the security boundary explicit instead of implicit.

sections.heading: Security: Least-Privilege IAM, Workload Identity & Cross-Account Access
sections.summary: Covers the identity and network controls that make AI workloads bankable — IRSA/Pod Identity, secrets and encryption, and safe cross-account access patterns.

content.text: Security for this role isn't a checklist, it's the design constraint everything else operates inside. The two workload-identity mechanisms to know cold for EKS are IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA), which federates via an OIDC provider implicitly created per cluster and lets a Kubernetes service account assume an IAM role directly, and EKS Pod Identity, the newer model that removes the per-cluster OIDC setup in favor of a Pod Identity Agent DaemonSet. Both should be applied one-role-per-application — sharing a role across service accounts breaks least privilege because the broadest permission in the role applies to every workload using it.

headers: Why it matters for a bank
rows: No long-lived credentials in code or Terraform state
Per-environment/tenant KMS CMKs, key policies scoping which roles can decrypt
Data classification boundaries enforced cryptographically, not just by IAM
TLS everywhere; PrivateLink/VPC interface endpoints for Bedrock/SageMaker APIs
GenAI traffic never traverses the public internet — reduces PCI/regulatory scope
`sts:AssumeRole` with external ID + resource-based policies, no shared long-lived keys
Central platform account can act in workload accounts without credential sprawl
IRSA or Pod Identity, one role per service account
A compromised pod can't laterally escalate to another workload's permissions

items: PrivateLink + VPC interface endpoints for `bedrock-runtime` and `bedrock-agent-runtime` keep model invocation traffic on the AWS backbone; pair with a Route 53 private hosted zone when doing cross-region Bedrock PrivateLink so DNS resolves to the private endpoint, not the public one.

Automate security controls as policy-as-code inside the pipeline (Conftest/OPA against the Terraform plan) so a misconfigured security group or public S3 bucket fails the PR, not a post-deploy audit finding.
For cross-account evidence and audit, lean on AWS Config conformance packs and Security Hub aggregation into the Audit account — auditors want continuous evidence, not a point-in-time review.

Guardrails' step-level checks (2026 `InvokeGuardrailChecks` API) are a security control too — they inspect tool arguments and generated code for injected instructions, which matters once agents can call action-group Lambdas with model-generated parameters.

interviewQA.q: IRSA or EKS Pod Identity — which would you pick for a new cluster and why?
interviewQA.a: For a brand-new cluster I'd lean toward Pod Identity because it removes the need to set up and manage a per-cluster OIDC identity provider — the Pod Identity Agent handles the credential vending, which is simpler to operate at scale across many clusters. That said, IRSA is more mature and I'd keep using it where I already have OIDC federation wired up for cross-account access patterns, since ripping that out for an existing cluster isn't worth the churn. Either way, the non-negotiable part is one IAM role per application/service account — never a shared role across workloads.

interviewQA.q: How do you design cross-account access from a central platform account into workload accounts without creating a security hole?
interviewQA.a: No long-lived shared credentials, ever. The platform account's automation assumes a role in the target account via `sts:AssumeRole`, scoped with an external ID and a trust policy that only allows that specific platform role to assume it. On the workload-account side, the assumed role itself is scoped to exactly what the platform needs to do there — deploy infrastructure, read specific tags — nothing broader. I'd also put a permission boundary on that role so even if its policy is later widened by mistake, it can't exceed the boundary.

interviewQA.q: Why put Bedrock traffic behind PrivateLink instead of just relying on IAM for security?
interviewQA.a: IAM controls who can call the API, but PrivateLink controls where the traffic physically goes — without it, even an authorized call to `bedrock-runtime` traverses the public internet path to reach the regional endpoint. For a bank, keeping that traffic on the AWS backbone via VPC interface endpoints materially reduces compliance scope for things like PCI, and it closes off a whole class of network-level exfiltration risk. IAM and PrivateLink are complementary controls, not substitutes for each other.

interviewQA.q: Describe how you'd prevent an over-permissioned Bedrock agent from becoming a security incident.
interviewQA.a: I'd scope the agent's execution role down to exactly the actions and specific resource ARNs it needs — invoke this one agent, retrieve from this one Knowledge Base — using resource-level IAM conditions, not a wildcard `bedrock:*`. I'd also enable the step-level guardrail checks so tool calls and any code the model generates get inspected before execution, since a prompt-injection attack against an agent typically tries to get it to call a Lambda action group with attacker-chosen parameters. And I'd log every invocation to CloudWatch/S3 so if something does go wrong, there's a full audit trail of what the agent actually did.

interviewQA.q: How do you automate security control evidence for auditors instead of doing manual reviews?
interviewQA.a: I push as much as possible into AWS Config conformance packs and Security Hub, aggregated centrally into the Audit account, so compliance posture is continuously evidenced rather than captured in a point-in-time spreadsheet. On the delivery side, policy-as-code checks in the CI pipeline — OPA/Conftest against the Terraform plan — mean a lot of what an auditor would otherwise sample for gets enforced before merge and is provable from pipeline logs. That combination turns 'show me your control evidence' into a report I can generate, not a fire drill.

sections.heading: API & Connectivity: API Gateway vs Kong
sections.summary: Covers the concrete tradeoffs between AWS's native managed gateway and Kong's self-hosted model, plus the network patterns (VPC, Route 53, Direct Connect) that connect it all to the rest of the bank.

content.text: This is a 'know both well enough to defend a choice' topic, not a 'pick a favorite' topic — a fintech platform team typically runs both, using each where its tradeoffs actually fit.

rows: Fully managed, serverless, AWS operates it
Self-hosted (or Konnect-managed) — you deploy and run it, full control over internals
Sub-1-2ms typical — lightweight NGINX/OpenResty reverse proxy
AWS-native serverless apps prioritizing speed of delivery over fine-grained control
Multi-cloud/hybrid estates, sub-ms latency needs, deep plugin customization
Native, first-class Lambda/Step Functions/VPC Link integration
Requires explicit integration work, though AWS-agnostic by design
Usage plans, API keys, request validation, WAF integration
Large plugin ecosystem incl. AI Gateway plugins for LLM traffic (semantic caching, prompt guarding, token-based rate limiting)
Real — you patch, scale, and secure the gateway layer yourself

items: Use API Gateway as the default front door for AWS-native, serverless-first services — it's the fastest path to a secured, auto-scaled API and integrates cleanly with private VPC Links so it never needs a public backend.

Reach for Kong when the estate spans multiple clouds or has significant on-prem legacy integration (common in a bank migrating off a mainframe/core-banking system), or when you need fine-grained LLM-traffic controls — token-bucket rate limiting per model, semantic response caching, prompt-injection screening at the gateway layer — that go beyond what API Gateway's usage plans offer.

Network foundation underneath both: Direct Connect (private VIF) or Site-to-Site VPN into a Transit Gateway hub gives on-prem systems a private path to AWS; Route 53 private hosted zones plus VPC interface endpoints keep DNS resolution for AWS service traffic (including Bedrock) off the public internet, and Route 53 itself now supports PrivateLink for its own API calls.

For hybrid banking environments specifically, expect to justify subnetting strategy (isolated subnets per tier: gateway, agent runtime, data), and how Transit Gateway route tables enforce which spokes can reach which shared services.

interviewQA.q: How would you decide between API Gateway and Kong for a new AI-agent-facing API?
interviewQA.a: First question is whether this API needs to be reachable from outside AWS or from another cloud — if it's purely AWS-native and serverless, API Gateway gets me a secured, scaled endpoint with almost no operational burden, and its native Lambda and VPC Link integration is hard to beat for speed of delivery. If we need multi-cloud reach, sub-millisecond latency, or LLM-specific traffic controls like token-aware rate limiting and semantic caching, I'd reach for Kong, accepting that we now own patching and scaling the gateway ourselves. In practice a platform this size usually runs both, each fronting the workloads it fits.

interviewQA.q: What does Kong's 'AI Gateway' capability give you that a plain reverse proxy wouldn't?
interviewQA.a: It adds LLM-aware plugins on top of standard API management — things like semantic response caching so repeated similar prompts don't all hit the model, prompt-injection screening at the gateway before a request even reaches the agent, and rate limiting based on token consumption rather than just request count, which matters a lot when your cost driver is tokens, not requests. That's meaningfully different from a generic reverse proxy, and it's the kind of feature that would tip me toward Kong specifically for LLM-facing traffic even in an otherwise AWS-native shop.

interviewQA.q: How do you keep Bedrock API traffic off the public internet in a hybrid network?
interviewQA.a: VPC interface endpoints powered by PrivateLink for `bedrock-runtime` and `bedrock-agent-runtime`, so calls resolve to a private ENI in my VPC instead of the public endpoint. If I'm calling cross-region, I pair that with a Route 53 private hosted zone that aliases the Bedrock domain name to the cross-region PrivateLink endpoint's DNS name, so the private path is fully honored end to end. For on-prem systems that need to reach these APIs, that same private path extends over Direct Connect private VIF or VPN into a Transit Gateway, so nothing ever touches the public internet.

interviewQA.q: Explain your VPC subnetting approach for an AI agent platform.
interviewQA.a: I isolate by tier and by trust boundary — public-facing gateway components (if any) in a dedicated subnet with tight security groups, agent runtime and Lambda in private subnets with no direct internet route, and data stores like the vector store or RDS in an even more isolated data subnet reachable only from the agent tier. Each tier gets its own route table so a Transit Gateway or NAT misconfiguration in one tier can't accidentally open a path from another. I also reserve enough CIDR space up front — re-subnetting a live VPC is painful, and AI workloads tend to grow subnet consumption fast as teams add Lambda ENIs and interface endpoints.

interviewQA.q: A legacy core-banking system needs to call a new Bedrock-backed API. How do you connect it?
interviewQA.a: I wouldn't expose the API publicly for that. I'd extend Direct Connect private VIF connectivity from the on-prem network into the AWS Transit Gateway, route it to the VPC hosting the API (behind either API Gateway with a VPC Link or Kong running in that VPC), and keep DNS resolution private through Route 53 Resolver rules so the on-prem system resolves the same private endpoint. That gives the legacy system a private, low-latency path without it ever leaving the bank's controlled network boundary — which is usually a hard requirement from the network security team anyway.

sections.heading: FinOps & Monitoring for AI Workloads
sections.summary: Covers the specific cost mechanics of generative AI (Bedrock's billing modes, runaway agent risk) and how to build alerting that catches problems before the invoice does.

content.text: AI workloads break the usual FinOps playbook because cost scales with usage patterns that are much harder to predict than CPU-hours — a single mis-behaving agent stuck in a retry loop can generate a meaningful spend spike in hours, not weeks. The FinOps Foundation's 2026 State of FinOps report found 98% of organizations now actively manage AI spend specifically, up from 31% two years earlier — this has become a distinct discipline, not a subset of general cloud cost management.

rows: Output tokens typically cost 3-4x input tokens — optimize prompt/response length
Reserved capacity — cheaper at sustained scale, wasteful if under-utilized
Up to ~90% savings on the cached portion
Custom-tuned model on top of a foundation model
One-time training cost + ongoing inference cost for the custom model

items: Turn on Bedrock's granular cost attribution (2026 feature) to break spend down by application, agent, and even session/user — without it, chargeback to business units is guesswork.

AWS Cost Anomaly Detection (ML-based, no manual thresholds to tune) is the right tool for catching a runaway agent loop or a sudden usage spike before it becomes an invoice surprise — pair it with SNS/Slack alerting so someone sees it within minutes, not at month-end.

CloudWatch custom metrics on token consumption per application, plus budgets and alarms at both the account and tag level, give you a second, real-time layer underneath the (often delayed) Cost Explorer view.

Savings Plans (Compute Savings Plans) apply to the steady-state EKS/Fargate/Lambda compute underneath your agent runtime, and SageMaker has its own Savings Plans for predictable inference endpoint usage — Bedrock on-demand itself isn't covered by Savings Plans, which is why provisioned throughput and prompt caching are the primary levers there instead.

Enforce mandatory cost-allocation tags via SCP/policy-as-code so every Bedrock/SageMaker/EKS resource is attributable from day one — retrofitting tagging onto an already-sprawling AI estate is much harder than starting with it.

interviewQA.q: How would you prevent a runaway agent loop from turning into a surprise six-figure Bedrock bill?
interviewQA.a: Multiple layers, because no single control is enough. First, hard guardrails in the application itself — a max-iteration cap on any agent loop, enforced in code, not just hoped for. Second, AWS Cost Anomaly Detection watching Bedrock spend with ML-based thresholds, wired to page the platform team via SNS within minutes of an abnormal spike, not at end of month. Third, CloudWatch alarms on token-consumption custom metrics per application, so I can correlate a spend spike with the specific agent causing it using the 2026 granular cost-attribution data, and kill or throttle it directly.

interviewQA.q: Walk me through the different Bedrock billing modes and when you'd use each.
interviewQA.a: On-demand is the default, pay-per-token mode, fine for unpredictable or low-volume traffic, but output tokens run three to four times the cost of input tokens so prompt and response length both matter. Batch gives roughly a 50% discount for anything that isn't latency-sensitive — nightly document summarization is a good fit. Provisioned throughput is a reserved-capacity model that pays off once you have predictable, high, sustained volume — I'd only commit to it after seeing real production traffic patterns, since it's wasted spend if utilization is low. And prompt caching can cut costs up to 90% on the portion of a request that's repeated system prompt or context, which is nearly free money for any agent that reuses the same instructions across calls.

interviewQA.q: How do you attribute AI spend back to individual business units for chargeback?
interviewQA.a: I enforce mandatory cost-allocation tags — business unit, application, environment — at the platform level via policy-as-code, so nothing gets provisioned untagged in the first place. On top of that I turn on Bedrock's granular cost-attribution capability, which breaks spend down to the application, agent, and even session level, and feed that into Cost Explorer's Cost Categories so finance gets a report that maps to how the bank actually organizes budgets, not just to AWS account boundaries.

interviewQA.q: Do Savings Plans help reduce Bedrock costs?
interviewQA.a: Not directly — Bedrock on-demand isn't covered by Compute Savings Plans, so the levers there are provisioned throughput for sustained volume and prompt caching for repeated context, not a Savings Plan commitment. Where Savings Plans do help is the compute underneath the platform — the EKS nodes or Lambda concurrency running your agent orchestration layer, and SageMaker has its own Savings Plans for steady-state inference endpoints. Part of my job is making sure teams don't conflate 'we bought a Savings Plan' with 'our GenAI costs are optimized' — those are different cost surfaces.

interviewQA.q: What CloudWatch-based monitoring would you put in place for an AI platform from day one?
interviewQA.a: Custom metrics for token consumption per application and per model, alarms on both absolute spend thresholds and rate-of-change so a sudden spike trips before it becomes a trend, and dashboards that put latency, error rate, and cost side by side so on-call engineers see the full picture, not just uptime. I'd also alarm on dead-letter-queue depth for the event-driven parts of the pipeline, since a backlog there is often the earliest signal that something downstream — including cost-driving retries — has gone wrong.

sections.heading: Telling Your Story: Framing Your Experience for a Regulated Fintech
sections.summary: How to translate general platform-engineering experience into language that lands with a bank's AI Center of Excellence — behavioral and system-design questions with model answers.

content.text: The gap between a good platform engineer and a good candidate for this specific role is framing: every story should connect a technical decision to a business constraint a regulated bank actually has — audit evidence, blast-radius containment, cost predictability, or developer velocity under governance. Avoid generic 'I built infrastructure' narratives; anchor each answer in who consumed the platform and what governance constraint shaped the design.

rows: A time you designed account/tenancy structure to satisfy a specific compliance boundary
A build-vs-buy call between a managed AI service and a custom model, with the reasoning
A module versioning or release-management decision that prevented a breaking change from cascading
An incident, near-miss, or audit finding you resolved by tightening IAM/network design
A cost anomaly you caught (or missed) and what monitoring you put in place afterward

items: Lead with the constraint, not the tool: 'The bank needed X because of Y regulation/risk, so I built Z' reads far stronger than 'I used Terraform and Bedrock to build Z.'

Be explicit about tradeoffs you accepted — interviewers trust a candidate more when they name what they gave up (e.g. slower initial delivery for stronger tenant isolation) than one who claims a decision was free.

Have one story ready where you pushed back on a request (a team wanting a shortcut around a security control, a shared IAM role for convenience) and held the line — this role has real authority over what gets rubber-stamped into a regulated bank's cloud estate.
Have one story ready where a platform decision aged badly and you had to migrate consumers off it — shows you understand that 'platform as a product' includes deprecation, not just launch.

interviewQA.q: Tell me about a platform or reusable infrastructure component you built that multiple teams ended up adopting.
interviewQA.a: At a previous role I built a versioned Terraform module set for standing up a governed EKS-based service runtime — VPC, IRSA-scoped IAM, ingress, and CI/CD wiring in one apply. The reason it got adopted broadly rather than becoming shelfware was that I treated it like a product from day one: semantic versioning, a changelog, and a Service Catalog entry so teams could self-serve without reading the module's internals. Within two quarters it was the default path for new services, and the real payoff showed up when a security requirement changed — I rolled it out as a version bump to every consumer instead of chasing down a dozen teams individually.

interviewQA.q: Describe a time you had to balance a business unit's request for speed against the bank's security or compliance requirements.
interviewQA.a: A team wanted to share one broad IAM role across several microservices to save setup time ahead of a deadline. I pushed back, because a shared role directly breaks least privilege — if one service is compromised, the blast radius is every service using that role, not just the one attacker touched. Instead I gave them a fast path: a pre-validated Terraform module that could generate a scoped role per service in minutes, so the 'slow' secure option became just as fast as the shortcut they were asking for. That's usually the actual resolution to this kind of tension — remove the reason speed and security are in conflict, rather than picking one over the other.

interviewQA.q: Tell me about a cost or operational incident you caught — or didn't catch in time — involving an AI or cloud workload.
interviewQA.a: A batch document-processing job started retrying on a subset of malformed inputs without a cap, and because it was calling a foundation model per attempt, the spend climbed for several hours before Cost Anomaly Detection flagged it — later than I'd have liked, because at the time we didn't have a token-consumption CloudWatch alarm at the application level, only account-level budget alerts. Afterward I added a hard retry cap in the application code, a dead-letter queue for anything that failed repeatedly, and a tighter, app-scoped CloudWatch alarm so the same failure mode would be caught within minutes next time rather than hours. I'd rather describe the gap honestly than pretend every control was already in place.

interviewQA.q: How would you design an AI agent platform for a bank that needs to serve five different business units with different compliance requirements?
interviewQA.a: I'd start from the landing zone: a hub account for shared, hard-to-replicate primitives like Guardrails policy and vector stores, and per-business-unit workload accounts vended through Account Factory for Terraform so each unit gets its own IAM and network boundary. Everything provisions through the same versioned Terraform module catalog so operational consistency doesn't depend on which team is building. Units with stricter compliance needs — say, one handling card data — get an account with tighter SCPs and their own KMS keys rather than being forced into the shared hub for anything sensitive. And I'd instrument cost and Guardrail policy centrally from day one, because retrofitting either onto five already-live business units is much harder than starting with it.

interviewQA.q: What's the hardest tradeoff you've had to defend to a security or compliance team, and how did you make the case?
interviewQA.a: Choosing EKS Pod Identity over continuing with IRSA on a new cluster, when the security team's existing audit tooling was built around IRSA's OIDC federation model. I made the case by showing that Pod Identity still gives us the same least-privilege, one-role-per-workload guarantee — it just changes how the credential is vended, not what it's scoped to — and I committed to updating our Config rules and audit queries to recognize the new model before rollout, rather than asking them to just trust it. Getting compliance buy-in usually isn't about winning an argument, it's about doing the work to show the new approach meets the same control objective, in language their audit framework already understands.

interviewQA.q: Why do you want to work in a bank's AI Center of Excellence specifically, rather than a less regulated tech company?
interviewQA.a: Honestly, the constraints are what make the engineering interesting to me — anyone can wire up a Bedrock agent over a weekend, but doing it in a way that survives a regulatory audit, keeps blast radius contained across business units, and doesn't blow a FinOps budget is a genuinely harder and more durable problem. I also think the platform-as-a-product model matters more here than in a smaller shop, because the cost of every team reinventing security and IAM patterns independently is much higher at bank scale. That's the kind of leverage I want my work to have.
